intro: Oregon paychecks can carry several state-related deductions because income tax sits alongside transit, Paid Leave, and WBF. This Oregon paycheck calculator separates those payroll components while applying the state's graduated 2026 formula.
taxSummary: Oregon uses graduated income-tax brackets from 4.75% to 9.9%, administered by the Oregon Department of Revenue. The calculator applies the "Oregon 2026 formula + transit, Paid Leave, and WBF." This means Oregon income-tax withholding is calculated separately from state payroll premiums that may also appear on the check. The examples show both categories, making it possible to distinguish the graduated income-tax amount from the additional Oregon payroll programs included in the calculation.

sections.h3: Why Oregon paychecks show deductions beyond state income tax
sections.p: Oregon's paycheck calculation contains more than the graduated income-tax line. The method used here also includes transit, Paid Leave, and WBF, with the additional amounts represented as state payroll premiums. At $45,000 single, Oregon state income tax is $128.64 while state payroll premiums are $12.11. At $65,000 single, those amounts become $177.75 and $17.50. Keeping them separate matters because the payroll premiums are not simply another Oregon income-tax bracket. When reviewing a paycheck, look at the state income-tax amount and the additional state payroll components independently rather than combining every Oregon-related deduction into a single tax percentage.

sections.h3: Oregon's $90,000 married paycheck line by line
sections.p: At $90,000 married filing jointly, biweekly gross pay is $3,461.54. Federal income tax removes $247.69, Social Security removes $214.62, and Medicare removes $50.19. Oregon state income tax is $237.09, while state payroll premiums add another $24.23. The resulting paycheck is $2,687.72 and annual net pay is $69,880.79. The effective state rate is 7.55%. At $130,000 married filing jointly, Oregon income tax rises to $363.93 and state payroll premiums become $35.00. Separating those two Oregon amounts shows which part comes from the graduated income-tax calculation and which part comes from the additional payroll programs.

sections.h3: How Oregon's graduated brackets interact with filing circumstances
sections.p: Oregon's brackets range from 4.75% to 9.9%, but the effective state rates in the examples do not simply climb in salary order. The $45,000 single case shows an 8.13% effective state rate, while $65,000 single shows 7.81%. At $90,000 married filing jointly, it is 7.55%, before rising to 7.98% at $130,000 married filing jointly. Filing circumstances and the Oregon withholding formula therefore matter alongside income. A headline bracket rate is not enough to reconstruct the paycheck deduction. Use the appropriate payroll setup and let the graduated calculation determine the Oregon state line rather than assigning one effective percentage to every worker.

sections.h3: What pre-tax benefits can change in an Oregon calculation
sections.p: The four Oregon salary examples contain no 401(k) contribution and no pre-tax benefits. If an employer-plan deduction changes the wages subject to Oregon income-tax withholding, the state income-tax result can differ from these examples. That effect should be kept conceptually separate from transit, Paid Leave, and WBF, which are included in the calculator method as additional state payroll components. Oregon's graduated structure makes taxable wages particularly relevant because a change in the amount entering the state formula does not necessarily produce a perfectly proportional change in withholding. Represent qualifying payroll deductions according to their treatment before comparing your Oregon income-tax line with a reference salary.

sections.h3: Oregon hourly workers can see several state lines move together

Variable hours change the gross wages entering the state formula, so the Oregon income-tax amount can move between checks. The additional payroll components represented by transit, Paid Leave, and WBF may also change with the payroll inputs. The salary examples avoid this variation by using 26 biweekly periods and fixed gross wages. For hourly work, calculate the actual period instead of dividing an annual Oregon estimate into equal checks. That approach keeps the graduated income-tax calculation and the additional state payroll deductions tied to the wages being modeled.

intro: South Carolina's graduated brackets are applied after allowances and standard deductions shape taxable wages. This South Carolina paycheck calculator uses the WH-1603F 2026 annualized formula rather than applying the 6.2% top rate to an entire check.

The higher salary therefore produces both a larger dollar deduction and a higher effective state percentage. That progression reflects the graduated calculation rather than a flat percentage being applied to each additional dollar of gross wages.

sections.p: Allowances and standard deductions reduce the taxable wages used by South Carolina's withholding calculation. That is one reason the effective percentages in the examples do not match the state's 6.2% top rate. The WH-1603F method annualizes the payroll information and then applies the state formula to the resulting taxable amount. If your withholding setup changes, the South Carolina line can change even without a corresponding change in gross salary. Focus on the wages entering the state calculation rather than treating gross pay as the only relevant number. This distinction becomes more important as income rises because the state uses graduated brackets rather than one common withholding percentage.
